nameStory: The Long-bodied Cellar Spider gets its name from its exceptionally skinny, elongated body and its love of cool, damp indoor spaces like cellars and basements. You might also hear it called a 'daddy long-legs spider,' though this nickname causes plenty of confusion since several completely different creatures share that same common name!
description: This delicate spider looks like it's been stretched on a medieval rack, with an incredibly thin, pale body and legs that seem impossibly long and spindly. Females grow to about 8mm in body length (roughly the size of a small pea), while males are slightly smaller. What's truly remarkable is that their legs can be 5-6 times longer than their body, giving them a total leg span that can reach across a quarter coin.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated, cylindrical body that feels papery-thin and fragile, like a dried twig that might snap if you breathed on it too hard

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates messy, irregular cobwebs in corners that feel sticky and collect dust easily, often with the spider hanging upside down in the center

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, rapidly vibrates its web so fast it becomes a blur, creating a buzzing sensation you can almost feel in the air

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny pea-sized body with disproportionately long, thread-like legs that span wider than a quarter when fully extended

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-brown to gray coloration with subtle darker patterns that look like watercolor stains on tissue paper

habitat: You'll find these spiders almost exclusively indoors throughout New England, particularly in undisturbed areas like basements, cellars, garages, and attics. They prefer cool, humid spaces with stable temperatures and often hang out on ceilings and in corners where their webs won't be disturbed. Occasionally they'll set up shop in caves or other naturally sheltered areas.

seasonality.spring: Active indoors year-round, with increased web-building activity as temperatures warm and prey insects become more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with frequent web maintenance and hunting behavior easily observed in basement corners and garage ceilings.
seasonality.fall: Continues normal activity indoors while outdoor temperatures drop, often more noticeable as people spend more time in basements and enclosed spaces.
seasonality.winter: Remains active in heated buildings, taking advantage of being one of the few spiders that doesn't need to overwinter dormant.

funFact: Despite looking incredibly fragile, these spiders are actually fierce predators that specialize in hunting other spiders - including species much larger and more dangerous than themselves, like black widows, which they can safely subdue with their long reach and specialized hunting technique.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with harvestmen (also called daddy long-legs), but cellar spiders have a distinct waist between their front and back body sections while harvestmen look like they have one rounded body. Remember: if it has a web and a 'wasp waist,' it's the spider; if it's wandering around without a web and looks like a pill with legs, it's a harvestmen.
contextualKnowledge: The 'daddy long-legs' name creates endless confusion because it refers to at least three completely different creatures: cellar spiders (true spiders), harvestmen (different arachnids entirely), and crane flies (which aren't even arachnids but insects). When someone mentions daddy long-legs, always ask what they're really talking about!
compareHints: Long-bodied Cellar Spiders are the most common cellar spider in New England homes and have the most extremely elongated body proportions. Other Pholcus species in the region are much less common and typically have slightly shorter legs relative to their body size. The vibrating defense behavior when disturbed is particularly pronounced in this species compared to its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Manuel's Cellar Spider is very similar to the Long-bodied Cellar Spider, and they're nearly impossible to tell apart without microscopic examination.

Distinguishing this species from its close relative, the Long-bodied Cellar Spider, requires very close examination of body proportions and leg length ratios that are difficult to assess in the field.
Compared to the common Long-bodied Cellar Spider, crypticolens is generally smaller and more pale in coloration.
